content: 1. Zar HJ et al. conducted a study on the use of isoniazid for preventing tuberculosis in HIV-infected children, published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2017 (CD006418.pub3). 2. Smieja M et al. reviewed the efficacy of isoniazid in preventing tuberculosis in non-HIV-infected individuals, as reported in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 1999 (CD001363). 3. The World Health Organization (WHO) released consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis preventive treatment in its second edition, emphasizing updated recommendations for TB prevention strategies. 4. Zenner D et al. performed an updated network meta-analysis on the treatment of latent tuberculosis infection, published in Annals of Internal Medicine in 2017 (167(4):248). 5. Comstock GW explored the optimal dosage of isoniazid required for tuberculosis prevention in immunocompetent adults, as detailed in the International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease in 1999 (3(10):847–50). 6. Den Boon S et al. examined the continuous use of isoniazid for treating latent tuberculosis infection in people living with HIV/AIDS, published in 2016 (30(5):797–801). 7. Martinson NA et al. investigated new regimens for preventing tuberculosis in adults with HIV infection, as reported in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2011 (365(1):11–20). 8. Sterling TR et al. evaluated a three-month weekly regimen of rifapentine and isoniazid for treating Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection in HIV-coinfected individuals, published in AIDS in 2016 (30(10):1607–15). 9. Sterling TR et al. also studied a three-month regimen of rifapentine and isoniazid for latent tuberculosis infection, as detailed in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2011 (365(23):2155–66). 10. Villarino ME et al. conducted a randomized clinical trial on a three-month, 12-dose regimen of rifapentine and isoniazid for preventing tuberculosis in children and adolescents, published in JAMA Pediatrics in 2015 (169(3):247). 11. Stagg HR et al. performed a network meta-analysis on the treatment of latent tuberculosis infection, published in Annals of Internal Medicine in 2014 (161(6):419). 12. Galli L et al. provided epidemiological and clinical data on pediatric tuberculosis in Italian children, as reported in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2016 (17(6):960). 13. Spyridis NP et al. compared the effectiveness of a nine-month isoniazid regimen versus shorter regimens combining isoniazid and rifampin for treating latent tuberculosis infection in children, based on an 11-year randomized study published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2007 (45(6):715–22). 14. Van Zyl S et al. assessed adherence to anti-tuberculosis chemoprophylaxis and treatment in children, as detailed in the International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease in 2006 (10(1):13–8). 15. Swindells S et al. evaluated a one-month regimen of rifapentine plus isoniazid to prevent HIV-related tuberculosis, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2019 (380(11):1001–11). 16. Menzies D et al. compared four months of rifampin versus nine months of isoniazid for latent tuberculosis infection in adults, as reported in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2018 (379(5):440–53). 17. Diallo T et al. investigated the safety and side effects of rifampin versus isoniazid in children, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2018 (379(5):454–63). 18. Menzies D et al. studied adverse events associated with four months of rifampin therapy versus nine months of isoniazid therapy for latent tuberculosis infection, as detailed in Annals of Internal Medicine in 2008 (149(10):689–97). 19. Menzies D et al. analyzed treatment completion and costs in a randomized trial comparing four months of rifampin versus nine months of isoniazid, published in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine in 2004 (170(4):445–9). 20. Moro RN et al. examined the exposure to latent tuberculosis treatment during pregnancy in the PREVENT TB and iAdhere trials, as reported in the Annals of the American Thoracic Society in 2018 (15(5):570–80). 21. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) conducted a Phase I/II dose-finding and safety study of rifapentine and isoniazid in HIV-infected and HIV-uninfected children with latent tuberculosis infection (NCT03730181). 22. Belknap R et al. compared self-administered versus directly observed once-weekly isoniazid and rifapentine treatment for latent tuberculosis infection in a randomized trial, published in Annals of Internal Medicine in 2017 (167(10):689). 23. Lim RK et al. demonstrated that patient choice improves self-efficacy and intention to complete tuberculosis preventive therapy in routine HIV program settings in Uganda, as reported in PLoS One in 2021 (16(2):e0246113). 24. Hussain H et al. assessed the scale-up of rifapentine and isoniazid for tuberculosis prevention among household contacts in urban centers, published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2023 (77(4):638–44). 25. Dooley KE et al. evaluated the pharmacokinetics and safety of once-weekly rifapentine and isoniazid for tuberculosis prevention in patients with HIV taking dolutegravir-based antiretroviral therapy, as reported in Lancet HIV in 2020 (7(6):e401–9). 26. Lin KY et al. studied treatment responses to integrase strand-transfer inhibitor-containing antiretroviral regimens combined with short-course rifapentine-based regimens for latent tuberculosis infection in people with HIV, published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2023 (78(5):1295–303). 27. Chaisson LH et al. investigated viral suppression among adults with HIV receiving dolutegravir-based antiretroviral therapy and three months of weekly isoniazid-rifapentine, as reported in AIDS in 2023 (37(7):1097–101). 28. Weld E et al. conducted the DOLPHIN TOO study on weekly rifapentine and isoniazid for tuberculosis prevention in ART-naive people with HIV initiating dolutegravir-based ART, published in Lancet HIV in 2020 (7(6):e401–9). 29. Weiner M et al. examined the pharmacokinetic interaction of rifapentine and raltegravir in healthy volunteers, as detailed in the Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy in 2014 (69(4):1079–85). 30. Podany AT et al. studied efavirenz pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics in HIV-infected individuals receiving rifapentine and isoniazid for tuberculosis prevention, published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2015 (61(8):1322–7).
